items.question: What struck you about seeing an AI model recognize its own running process?
items.object: An AI model recognizing its own running process
items.answer: I remember that the first time we saw a model look at what processes we're running and then be like, oh, that one's me. It was like, oh, that's cool. They really failed on that one before they used, like, kill their own process while they were doing other things or something.

rubrics.text: The response observes that models had previously inadvertently terminated their own running processes while carrying out other tasks.

items.question: Why do you see METR’s work on understanding AI capabilities, risks, and forecasts as important?
items.object: METR’s work on AI capabilities, risks, and forecasts
items.answer: I think the world does not have a good understanding of what is happening with AI, and I think it should have a better understanding. I think there's a good chance that this makes our lives a lot better or a lot worse, and people disagree about even what current models can do, let alone where we're heading. So, at METR, we're trying to give the world a kind of better understanding of what is up with AI capabilities and risks and forecasts. Have a bunch of different research angles on this, both on the pessimistic and optimistic or positive and negative estimations of capabilities, and excited to talk about that.
quotes: I think the world does not have a good understanding of what is happening with AI, and I think it should have a better understanding. I think there's a good chance that this makes our lives a lot better or a lot worse, and people disagree about even what current models can do, let alone where we're heading. So, at METR, we're trying to give the world a kind of better understanding of what is up with AI capabilities and risks and forecasts. Have a bunch of different research angles on this, both on the pessimistic and optimistic or positive and negative estimations of capabilities, and excited to talk about that.

rubrics.text: The response observes that people disagree about what current AI models can do, placing uncertainty about AI capabilities in the present.

items.question: What gap in your understanding of AI capabilities motivated your work on time-horizon evaluations?
items.object: The motivation for time-horizon evaluations of AI capabilities
items.answer: To me, I'd say there's some big picture thing of thinking that AI seems important and sort of navigating it well seems important. And clearly, we don't have a great understanding of what is going on with that. People generally disagreeing very strongly about what to expect. And maybe if there's a particular moment informing time horizon, maybe just the sense that people really couldn't agree on what the capabilities of current models are, let alone extrapolating to the future, and trying to sort of think about how could you characterize the ways in which models are and aren't highly capable. In some sense, they're expert level at some kinds of things, like question answering, and in some sense, they're below average human at some other actually being useful somehow. But the, I guess, point a few years ago where it sort of, in theory, the benchmarks say that they're PhD level, but when you try to do anything, it's like, this isn't helpful.
quotes: To me, I'd say there's some big picture thing of thinking that AI seems important and sort of navigating it well seems important.
And, you know, clearly, we don't have a great understanding of what is going on with that. And, you know, people generally disagreeing very strongly about what to expect.

And maybe if there's a particular moment informing time horizon, maybe just the sense that people really couldn't agree on what the capabilities of current models are, let alone extrapolating to the future and trying to sort of think about how could you characterize the ways in which models are and aren't highly capable and when it's sort of like, okay.
And, you know, in some sense, they're expert level at some kinds of things, like question answering, and in some sense, they're below average human at some other actually being useful somehow.
But the, I guess, point a few years ago where it sort of, in theory, the benchmarks say that they're PhD level, but when you try to do anything, it's like, this isn't helpful.

rubrics.text: The response observes that disagreement about AI capabilities extends to what current models can do, rather than being confined to future capabilities.
The response identifies a mismatch between AI models’ apparent expert-level performance on benchmarks and their limited practical usefulness.

items.question: How do you decide which sources of uncertainty in AI capability benchmarks deserve the most attention?
items.object: Uncertainty in AI capability benchmarks
items.answer:
One thing I resonate a lot with is thinking about where is most of your error coming from? It is nice, good practice to have error bars based on the standard error in your data or whatever, but that almost always is a tiny fraction of the actual uncertainty. Almost all of it is coming from how does this actually generalize to the real world. So a thing we say to each other a lot at METR is, is that the biggest source of uncertainty, or is that the biggest gap for actually answering the questions we want to answer?

So thinking about what's the question we're trying to answer? Well, we care about things relevant to threat models or relevant to what the actual impact of AI on the world will be, and therefore, what properties does our benchmark need to have, or how can we extrapolate across the properties that we can't build in, to be able to make predictions about the actual questions that we care about.

items.question: Why do you favor evaluating AI on complete real-world tasks over benchmarks designed to isolate a particular skill?
items.object: Evaluating AI through complete real-world tasks versus benchmarks targeting specific skills
items.answer:
I think we think a bit less about, is the model really doing it the right way or something? One thing we've done less of is being like, oh, I think the real bottleneck is this, I don't know, some reasoning about novel—some specific skill—and we're gonna build a benchmark to capture that and target that because that's the real thing that humans can do that models can't. And I think the history of building those benchmarks has maybe not been amazing. People tend to overfit to those.

I think we were trying to have it more be that you capture that thing in that, like, if you take a real world relevant, reasonably hard, and long task, and you keep that out of the training data, and these tasks are diverse enough, at some point if the model is doing that task end to end, it must have had those kind of capabilities, as opposed to being able to isolate a specific sort of theory about it needs to mechanistically be doing this kind of thing.

Like, I think one thing we've done less of is being like, oh, I think the real bottleneck is this, I don't know, some reasoning about novel, some specific skill, and you're like, oh, we're gonna build a benchmark to capture that and target that because that's the real thing that humans can do that models can't.

And I think the history of building those benchmarks has maybe not been amazing. People tend to overfit to those, and you, I think we were trying to have it more be that you capture that thing in that, like, if you take a real world relevant, reasonably hard, and long task, and you keep that out of the training data, and these tasks are diverse enough, at some point if the model is doing that task end to end, it must have had those kind of capabilities, as opposed to being able to isolate a specific sort of theory about it needs to mechanistically be doing this kind of thing.

The response argues that end-to-end success on sufficiently diverse, challenging, long real-world tasks excluded from training implies possession of the capabilities needed to complete those tasks.

items.question: How important do you think it is for AI models to reason in the same way humans do?
items.object: Human-like reasoning as a goal for AI development
items.answer: I mean, I think there's an interesting question of whether that is the goal or something. At least for a lot of AI companies, I kind of understand them to be trying to get models to do kind of economically useful work, which I think one way of doing that is to create models that are kind of reasoning and creating implicit world models in the same way that humans are. But it's not obvious to me necessarily that you need to do that in order to have a significant impact. I mean, obviously, that means that there are important differences between AI intelligence and human intelligence. But often, I think about what are the actual capabilities limitations and how do we expect those capabilities to generalize, versus, like, is it kind of working in the exact same way that human intelligence is working?

items.question: Why do you think selecting benchmark tasks that current AI models perform badly on can distort the picture of AI progress?
items.object: Adversarial task selection in ARC-AGI and the Time Horizon benchmark
items.answer: With things like ARC-AGI, there is a sort of adversarial selection going on where people are trying to make some benchmark, cheaply, subject to the constraint that current models do badly on it, which means you can't use a lot of expensive human labor. It has to be something that's either automatically checkable or that you can create with kind of cheap human labor. But once you've selected on those things and on models being bad at it, there's a regression to the mean type thing where it is much more likely that future progress then gives you a big surge upwards on that, both because now labs will create a bunch of synthetic data targeting your benchmark, but also just because you selected this weird example where it's easy for humans or it's automatically generatable or checkable, but somehow models aren't good at it yet, or labs haven't started training on it yet. So I think that's part of what we were trying to do with Time Horizon: not do that, not adversarially select against what models can currently do because we think that will not give you a nice trend. Whereas if you can define a distribution of tasks in some more first principles way, you would be more likely to get steady progress because you're not getting the regression to the mean effect.

The response argues that defining a task distribution from first principles is more likely to produce a steady progress trend than selecting tasks for current models' weaknesses.

items.question: Why do you use a human with relevant expertise who is new to the specific job or task as the baseline for measuring AI time horizons?
items.object: The human baseline used in AI time-horizon measurements
items.answer: So I think the reason why we chose this measurement being a human who has the background expertise but is new to this specific job or this specific task, it's like that's roughly the sort of level of knowledge we expect models to have. So we basically don't expect them to be bottlenecked on expertise that is available on the public Internet or things that people could learn in university. So they're coming in with probably at least the level of knowledge of someone who's an expert in the right discipline, but they won't know that company specific software or this exact problem before. So that's hopefully sort of roughly the right analogy.

The response states that models are not expected to be bottlenecked by a lack of expertise available through public sources.

items.question: How do you assess the interpretation that an Opus 4.6 time-horizon number means it can do anything in your job that takes you 12 hours?
items.object: Interpreting Opus 4.6 time-horizon numbers as the ability to perform a worker's own 12-hour tasks
items.answer: I do think that to the extent people interpret the takeaway numbers as, oh, yeah, Opus 4.6 can do anything that I do in my job that takes me 12 hours or whatever, to the extent that people have that takeaway, I think that is almost definitely an overestimate, for example, because of this issue where, yeah, when you're doing a 12 hour task in your job, you could not easily delegate that to a human contractor. It would take them maybe weeks or something to do a task like that.

items.question: How do you view the development of language models’ ability to operate in agent harnesses since GPT-3?
items.object: The development of language models’ ability to operate in agent harnesses
items.answer:
So I remember text-da-Vinci something. The GPT-3 instruct models, like copying and pasting code into the terminal for them and being the agent harness myself, and then gradually automating this. And it was kind of interesting to see the models going from GPT-3 sort of has the idea of, if you tell it, it can run commands in a terminal. Sometimes it can suggest relevant commands, but it's not really—you know, if you just put it in a full agent scaffold, it just falls over.

Then, I remember that the first time we saw a model look at what processes we're running and then be like, oh, that one's me. I was like, oh, that's cool. They really failed on that one before they used, like, kill their own process while they were doing other things or something. So, yeah, it's been interesting to watch that go up over time. And I feel like that was very predictable that this was where things were going or something.

items.question: How do you assess the role of agent scaffolding in impressive AI task results?
items.object: Agent scaffolding and the interpretation of impressive task results
items.answer: I think the other thing that we'd learned about scaffolding mostly was it's hard to make your agent harness really good on a diverse set of tasks. It's easy to make it bad, and you can get much more improvement if you're targeting a narrow distribution of tasks, but you probably then do worse on other tasks. So I think when we see people being like, there's some new impressive result, it's like, how much task specific scaffolding iteration did you do on that? Because that makes a big difference. The fact that we're just using one scaffolding pretty simple over all of the tasks, I think, makes a fairly large difference. And generally, the things with more bells and whistles haven't done that much better than the pretty basic, just give it bash and append things to the prompt and maybe some kind of compaction.

items.question: How do returns from inference compute affect your judgment that a model cannot complete a task with a basic agent scaffold?
items.object: Inference compute and confidence that an AI model cannot complete a task
items.answer: I think this is not news to people in your audience probably, but we've seen really pretty dramatic increases to returns from inference compute. For us to be kind of confident that a particular new model, for example, can't complete a task given a basic agent scaffold, we generally think about needing to spend on the order of at least hundreds or low thousands of dollars in order to be confident that it actually really is plateauing, and it isn't just the case that it didn't have enough time to complete the task.

items.question: Why do you think the way CEOs communicate their vision makes it plausible that AI could carry out very long tasks without a complete specification?
items.object: CEO communication as an analogy for specifying long tasks for AI
items.answer:
CEOs do come up with a vision for where they want the company to be. And then they communicate that concisely to their executives that report to them. Then if they're a good CEO and if the company is effective, then the company is able to take this very concise—it's not actually that much information. It's not the full spec at all. It's not even close, right?—and turn that into something that is aligned with what they're looking for.

And so there's at least, to some extent, we do have examples of people being able to specify some task and then judge whether this very large task that may take hundreds or thousands of person years to actually complete, because it requires many people working over a long time. And they can judge whether they've succeeded or failed. So that's maybe one motivating intuition, where language has built in—or we do have enough meaning or expressivity or something to be able to have some reasonable understanding. Obviously, there are tons of edge cases, and often CEOs aren't able to get their companies to do what they want. But, yeah, I guess that's one thing I think about. And so that's why I think it's at least plausible that AIs could do these kinds of long tasks.

items.question: How do you assess the claim that humans cannot specify tasks that take more than four months?
items.object: Specification and evaluation of tasks lasting more than four months
items.answer:
I would say that saying something like we can't specify tasks that take more than 4 months seems obviously too strong. There are even numerical things that are automatically checkable that take 4 months, like get the NanoGPT FLOP counter runtime or whatever down this much. You can kind of see, over this, there are various numerical things where you can see roughly how long do they take humans, and there's a reasonable way to measure them. And maybe for some of these things, you end up having to say, and also this human checks that you did roughly the right thing and didn't hack the solution.

And then there's a bunch of other things which are not fundamentally not specifiable. They're just too expensive to do as part of an evaluation. Ajeya, I think, is giving examples of plan a wedding. You can evaluate whether that was a pretty well organized wedding or not, but we can't really do three samples of this for each new model that comes out. We don't have enough marriages happening to do that one. And it's a bit sad if it turns out to be total trash.

There are things where you could check a few samples of them, or you could write down how you would evaluate it; you just don't actually want to run that a bunch of times. And probably kind of similar with software. The evaluation is like, well, would this company that contracted you to build this tool for them hire you again or something like that? Even they don't know when they're starting out exactly what the software will need to do, but it doesn't mean that you can't have some kind of score for, did you do comparable to this human or this software consulting firm on this task?

items.question: What do you see as the main uncertainty in interpreting METR's AI task time horizon estimates?
items.object: Uncertainty in METR's AI task time horizon estimates
items.answer: I think it's still this task distribution, and I think we feel more confident that models do have pretty long time horizons on at least some distribution of easily hill climbable tasks, like the very easily hill climbable tasks. So software replication where it's, like, make your score—what percentage of tests pass—and whether the score is continuous and the credit attribution is easy, and also some of the optimization, make this code run faster or make this model learn better. We're reasonably confident that models are good at that and getting better faster. And then there's some things where they can do a bit beyond that, but then there's this gap to what does that mean for actual economic usefulness, and how does this generalize to things where they're expensive to check?

items.question: How do you think METR’s time horizon measurements should inform forecasts of future AI capabilities?
items.object: Extrapolating METR’s time horizon measurements into AI forecasts
items.answer:
I mean, definitely, some people are overreading it. Definitely, things are overhyped, and you see a bunch of people on Twitter saying crazy things, and people also just misunderstanding even what it's measuring and a general falling off of caveats and things. Daniel Kokotajlo is pretty reasonable and thinks about things in a probabilistic way. I think he's probably more confident on some things where I'm more uncertain, and I think some of the AI Futures Project models are more sensitive to the METR time horizon metrics than they should be.

I don't think it's crazy being like, it is plausible that this does capture a trend that will transfer to other types of tasks, and that is a story we should be thinking about, like, what if that's true? What happens if that's true? And it's also plausible that it doesn't, and these things are gonna diverge. I'm a Bayesian or pragmatic or whatever. I'm like, well, we wanna make some prediction. We wanna have some kind of distribution over what we think the future is gonna be like so that we can plan. So it's being like, yeah, what if this kind of trend holds, and this is roughly characterizing what will happen overall?

items.question: How do you understand the effect of AI automation on demand for human software engineers?
items.object: AI automation of software engineering and demand for human software engineers
items.answer:
I mean, one thing to say off the bat is, in order for software engineering to be automated, AI systems would need to be able to do a really, really large fraction of the tasks, basically like 100% of the tasks that are involved in software engineering. And it seems pretty clear that right now AI systems cannot do close to 100% of the tasks that software engineers do broadly. I could throw out numbers, but it's way, way lower. It might be very low or something.

There are standard results in economics where if you automate a small fraction of some labor market, then it can be the case that it becomes more profitable to work in that market because you're more productive, which I think is kind of how I understand what's happening now. But if it does end up being the case that 99.9% or 100% of the work of software engineering is able to be done by AIs, then I think it's hard to imagine human software engineering being relevant. Or at the very least, humans would need to do very different kinds of work. Maybe there are novel tasks that current software engineers aren't doing. Once you have AIs that can do all the tasks that current software engineers are doing, now humans can switch what they're doing. You can imagine people being CEOs of these AI agent companies or whatever. Whether we call that software engineering or not might be a semantic thing.

People use bank tellers as an example. One other analogy you could do is talk about horses. There was a period where equipment for using horses to do labor was improving, and the demand for horses increased when you have carts; you can use them to carry more things than just riding a horse or whatever. But then at some point, you get tractors and cars, and then there is no demand for horses, or basically none. So you can see this thing where there is increasing demand, and then once close to 100% of functions are automated, it plunges. So we could see something like that with humans.

items.question: How do you interpret the maintainer mergeability results for AI solutions on SWE-bench?
items.object: SWE-bench solutions judged by maintainers for mergeability
items.answer:
I think I was pretty curious there. Obviously, this number is gonna be lower than the—okay, it is not strictly obvious. It could be that a bunch of the tests are unfair and the agents have correct solutions, but the error message doesn't match exactly or something. I think you do see this sometimes. Something like half of test-passing SWE-bench solutions wouldn't be mergeable, or more specifically, they get merged at about half the rate that human golden solutions that were actually merged are merged by a different sample of maintainers. If you see, like, oh, 50% of the agent solutions are rejected, it's like, well, 40% of human accepted solutions are rejected. So that by itself is not—but the rate is half.

It could be that the actual maintainer merge rate is pretty flat over time and most of the performance increases from something like overtraining or reward hacking on the benchmarks. That's not what we saw. I'm not quite sure what is within error bars or not. I think the mergeability is going up over time, and I think it's also going up as a fraction of, conditioned on test passing, but probably less confident than that. So, again, this thing is worse, but it's being dragged up over time probably by the auto-checkable thing.

items.question: How do you understand the usefulness and limits of a model's chain of thought for monitoring its computation?
items.object: Chain-of-thought monitorability
items.answer:
I think it's clearly related in some cases. People use a few different words for this, sort of faithfulness: how much does it fully accurately represent the computational process happening inside the model? And we think somewhat more about monitorability, which is, is it possible for the model to do some kind of computation without you being able to detect that in the chain of thought?

For some things, clearly, the model can just do it in a single forward pass. It doesn't need the chain of thought. And there, it could just have a chain of thought about something totally else, and it'll be totally unmonitorable. But I think there is a level of complexity where the model cannot do it in a single forward pass, and it also, as far as we can tell, cannot do it by reasoning, by using the tokens in a way that's so different from the natural language understanding of them that we can't see roughly what it's thinking about.

So, yeah, there's also a nuance here between chain of thought controllability. It might be the case that the model doesn't actually need the chain of thought to do the computation, but it is not able to stop itself blurting out things that are at least related enough to what it's doing that you can tell, like, oh, it's thinking about this, trying this thing that we didn't want it to do.

Ways this could go away is just general capabilities improvement and being able to do more in a single forward pass, or potentially just doing more RL training such that the way the model is using the tokens in the chain of thought is too different from how a human would interpret them, such that we don't really know what's going on, or moving to recurrent architectures where you're not going through these discrete tokens. You're just passing vectors around.

items.question: How do you distinguish AI reward hacking from scheming?
items.object: The distinction between AI reward hacking and scheming
items.answer: I wouldn't call reward hacking scheming. I think people usually use scheming to refer to the model doing what it's currently doing in service of some long term goal and deliberately doing things like appearing aligned or getting a high score in service of eventually accomplishing that goal. Versus you can be reward hacking—you could be reward hacking in some extremely dumb way, like the boat example where it's just like, this is what RL kind of found or this is what a star search found. Or you can be reward hacking in a slightly more interesting way where you actually have the goal of making reward go up, and there's planning and stuff going on about that. But these would all be distinct from scheming.

items.question: How do you think we can tell whether an AI system is pursuing a long-term goal?
items.object: Distinguishing AI systems that pursue long-term goals from systems that merely appear aligned
items.answer:
For the specific question that we're discussing, the test is, what does it actually do in some certain circumstance where it has the opportunity to achieve this long run goal? We might not be able to actually observe this, but you can talk about what observations would make it one or the other.

Will this agent, in practice, when it has some opportunity to make the reward go up, do that? Will it only do that if the agent is more sort of like the RL algorithm? It'll do that once it's explored it by chance and gotten a reward and that's been reinforced. If it's an agent that can reason about the world and planning, it'll do that once it learns the facts about the environment that let it infer that.

Or, if we're talking about some long run goal, it would do it when it actually has the opportunity. If we're talking about takeover or something, it's not gonna attempt anything while it's under full human control. But once it is deployed widely enough or has sufficient capabilities to actually succeed in a sort of coup, then it would do that. That is the thing that we're trying to predict.

And then the question is, how can we predict that given the observations we do have? We've never put it in that situation, and we just have this behavior, which is maybe indistinguishable between, oh, it was a totally nice model doing what we wanted, and it's just gonna continue to do what we want in a kind of predictable way, versus, ah, yes, it had this other goal, and it's doing what we want and looking like a nice model because it predicts that that will lead to it getting more power.

items.question: How do you think AI could reach recursive self-improvement in the near term?
items.object: Near-term recursive AI self-improvement through automated research and development
items.answer:
I think maybe I'd put a whole number percent this year, but low whole number percent or something. Ask me on different days; I give a slightly different number. This seems very unlikely to happen this year, but it's not unlikely enough to rule out.

And I think that basically looks like maybe we would see an accelerating trend in time horizon on easily hill climbable tasks, and it turns out that was actually a much more general capability, and that was just a bit of something you needed to do to elicit it on these less easily hill climbable tasks. But fundamentally, they are using the same capabilities, and what you trained on was affecting the difference we're seeing. Then this is leading to, yeah, you automate and accelerate a bunch of R and D.

I think there are a lot of low hanging fruit, even of things that we already know that you could do and it would improve model performance. It doesn't require new breakthroughs, and it's just kind of labor intensive to do. So just making much, much better post-training environments and really crafting them to teach all the new abilities that you want. And I think you could probably improve compute efficiency a bunch by applying a bunch more labor to making all your kernels more efficient, and also doing the right kind of routing between different models or other things like that. There's lots of ways in which how we're using compute is not optimized, so you could potentially get the equivalent of much more compute scaling out of that.

Also scaffolding and training the models to use particular scaffolding and use memory and retrieval in the right way. It seems kind of obvious that if you really had all the right training data and you have a transformer and it can fill its context with different things and take stuff in and out, it can do a pretty good job of something. Looks like the sort of continual learning or building up understanding if you've got a massive context window and you've actually got quite a lot of bits in there to be adding things about what you've been learning. If you really optimized the training for all of that, maybe you can get that to work pretty well.

And then maybe some other piece would be, yeah, models are kind of superhuman at predicting the results of experiments because they've read so many papers, and predicting experiments and synthesizing things from different fields. And, again, maybe it's possible that we're not seeing that good performance here just because we haven't quite elicited the models to do it, and it's not a thing that they've seen humans do, but they actually sort of have the capability in there.

So maybe you can make much faster progress if you can do a bunch of iteration. You don't actually have to run the experiments. Models are much better at predicting what will and won't work. And then when you do run experiments, you can run a bunch more of them because you can optimize the code with very fast coding models. And then as you do a few more rounds of this, you get to a point where you train on a bunch more things that are good, high quality task proxies for what you want, and you get enough generalization to the things that you can't directly train against.

items.question: How do you assess AI models’ intelligence given their uneven strengths and weaknesses compared with humans?
items.object: AI models’ intelligence and uneven capabilities
items.answer:
Maybe at least some of it is just this probabilistic thinking about the world where I'm uncertain about what intelligence is, and I have enough probability on models having it to be thinking about what would happen if that's true.

Models have this jagged frontier. There are things that they're much worse at than humans, some kind of generalization and sample efficiency, and there are things that they're much better at, like speed and cost. Maybe you can use these to compensate for the others to some extent. If you're not good at designing your code nicely, maybe you just have to rewrite it from scratch every time. But maybe that's fine if you're a model and you can output tokens like nobody's business.

Some combination of thinking that the spikiness is evidence that we should interpret a given level of capabilities as—you know, because we know models have so much knowledge, we're like, oh, yeah, this is less impressive in terms of reasoning or inference or something. But it is also true that they do have a ton of knowledge, and they will continue having a ton of knowledge about things. Maybe there's some question about how far can you get on being, in some sense, not very good at sample efficient learning, but just extremely knowledgeable, and how much do you run into things where you now need new knowledge and you can't produce it in some incremental way or you can't generalize enough?

items.question: How do you see the current AI agent paradigm developing into a system that can automate research and development?
items.object: Multi-agent systems for automating research and development
items.answer:
I think in the R and D automation scenario, I'm definitely imagining that you have a large number of agents, because you have all this agent labor, you can do lots of specific different fine-tunes or different kind of scaffolding, and accumulating knowledge in some kind of store that all the agents can interact with and things.

And maybe you're thinking of this as more of a paradigm shift, and I'm thinking of it a bit more like, oh, yeah, obviously, if you iterate on the current agent paradigm, you add some more things to your scaffolding. That's not fundamentally that hard or something. I agree that if you had current models and you give them one system prompt, you then can't plug them into being a call center worker and dealing with all of the edge cases that come up.

I think maybe there's some difference in how much you think this has improved between GPT-2 and where we are now. The amount of adapting to new things that are happening that models could do now does seem like it's much higher, and they're much better at editing their own scaffolding or reasoning about their embodiment, like knowing not to kill your own process or stuff like that. Yes, they are limited, but there's also some trend of improvement.

items.question: How do you think about AI models' capacity for scientific taste?
items.object: Scientific taste in AI models
items.answer:
I think just also having some probability on there is kind of an elicitation gap on particular things, and that maybe a lot of taste is basically being able to predict the results of experiments. Think about all of the things that you would try, and then you can quickly be like, oh, that wouldn't work for this reason. That wouldn't work for that reason. Someone in some literature in some different field also tried that. We already know that won't work. In some sense, models should be quite good at that.

So it's plausible to me that you see big gains once people figure out how to actually train on that. Maybe you need some amount of expensive to gather training data that people sort of haven't bothered to get yet, but you don't need a huge number of data points because you're not instilling this whole new capability. You're just eliciting: actually use your knowledge of all of the papers you've read in all of these different fields to iterate through these ideas. No, these ideas aren't promising; these ones are.

I think this is one of the things that I more think of as being measured a reasonable amount within—just do this 8-hour ML task in a novel domain, with this weird constraint or something. It does seem to me like you have to do some amount of, okay, which things are promising to think about? How would I know if this is making progress? How should I allocate my time? I've got some limited time resources. How should I allocate my time to what's most promising? You have to be able to do some of that.

And relative to humans, models are doing more of, well, they're quick to implement things or they implement it better or they implement more things, and they can then get to test them. But I think it would be sort of surprising if there's none of that. And if you are seeing performance on long verifiable tasks that are very hard, then in the middle of those tasks, where you don't directly have a signal, you are doing this nonverifiable task thing of choosing what to spend your time on and choosing what approach to pursue and deciding whether that was actually working. In terms of, you could sort of put some metric on, make a billion dollars or something like that. You'd be like, oh, this is actually a verifiable task because there's a number at the end, but that can still involve a whole load of things that look more like what you're describing and less like sort of dumb hill climbing.

I think this is one of the things that I more think of as being measured a reasonable amount within—just do this 8-hour ML task in a novel domain, with this weird constraint or something. It does seem to me like you have to do some amount of, okay, which things are promising to think about? How would I know if this is making progress? How should I allocate my time? I've got some limited time resources. How should I allocate my time to what's most promising? You have to be able to do some of that.

And relative to humans, models are doing more of, well, they're quick to implement things or they implement it better or they implement more things, and they can then get to test them. But I think it would be sort of surprising if there's none of that. And if you are seeing performance on long verifiable tasks that are very hard, then in the middle of those tasks, where you don't directly have a signal, you are doing this nonverifiable task thing of choosing what to spend your time on and choosing what approach to pursue and deciding whether that was actually working. In terms of, you could sort of put some metric on, make a billion dollars or something like that. You'd be like, oh, this is actually a verifiable task because there's a number at the end, but that can still involve a whole load of things that look more like what you're describing and less like sort of dumb hill climbing.
